newsitem.title: USA: Algerian being held by U.S. starts hunger strike.
newsitem.headline: Algerian being held by U.S. starts hunger strike.

text.p: A leading Algerian militant held by the United States said he began a hunger strike on Wednesday to press his case for political asylum or a chance to seek refuge abroad.

In a telephone interview from a jail in Manassas, Virginia, where he he has been held since December, Anwar Haddam of the banned Islamic Salvation Front said he would refuse all food "for as long as it takes" to be freed.

Haddam, who served as spokesman for the group in the United States, was detained by the U.S. Immigration and Naturalisation Service on Dec. 6 after the visa that had let him stay legally while awaiting a ruling on his asylum request had expired.

"It has been very difficult for my lawyers to find me another country (that would grant asylum) while I am in jail," he said. He accused unspecified Zionist "extremists," in league with the army-backed government in Algiers, of orchestrating the decision to deny him asylum.

Haddam was among 188 Islamic militants who won seats in Algeria's 430-member legislature in the first round of an election in December 1991. The Algerian Army cancelled a runoff in January 1992. That blocked almost certain victory by the Salvation Front, known by its initials in French as the FIS.

Haddam, calling himself a political prisoner, said he believed some U.S. officials had intervened with Sweden to thwart his plan to seek asylum there after an initial rejection by the United States in October.
He declined to name any other countries where he had sought refuge on the grounds that he would be in danger as "the main target of the military in Algeria."
Haddam said he condemned terrorism but supported "freedom fighting, the fight of our people to defend their elected institutions."
